articles.title: The skin-brain axis: New research highlights the link between mental well-being and skin health
articles.summary: A new study suggests a strong link between mental health struggles and skin conditions. Researchers found that stress and depression often accompany skin issues, particularly in women.

articles.title: Marking the Wrong Symptoms: Evaluating LLM Watermarks in Medical Texts
articles.summary: arXiv:2607.20462v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into clinical workflows, stressing the need for reliable traceability of model-generated output with watermarking. Yet, most watermarks are evaluated on general-purpose benchmarks, leaving domains like medicine, where small token-level perturbations can result in significant semantic changes, underexplored. articles.summary: arXiv:2607.20464v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When a language model gives different answers on repeated runs, does that variation reveal what it does not know? articles.title: PhantomFill: When the Form Demands an Answer, Language Models Invent One
articles.summary: arXiv:2607.20492v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language models in production do not write prose. They fill forms: JSON fields, function arguments, extraction templates. We show that the form itself causes hallucination. We ask thirteen models the same question about the same input and change only the answer format. The inputs are built so the question cannot be answered: a viral post showing 12,400 likes but no visible replies, a support ticket whose call was never transcribed. In free text, GPT-5.5 answers honestly. It says there is no reply data, 98% of the time. Given a required JSON field

articles.title: Scientists discover the hidden brain switch that assigns bees their jobs
articles.summary: Researchers found that specific brain circuits help decide which jobs bees perform as they age. When those circuits were switched off, older worker bees began caring for the queen again instead of carrying out their normal later-life duties. The findings reveal that a bee colony’s complex division of labor may be guided by neural switches hidden inside each bee’s brain.

articles.title: Lab-grown mini brains may predict which Alzheimer’s treatments will work
articles.summary: Miniature brain models grown from patients’ cells revealed striking differences in how Alzheimer’s-related tissue responds to an antidepressant. The organoids and the particles they release could eventually guide more personalized treatments and provide new clues for diagnosing the disease.

articles.title: High-achieving working mothers face harsher moral judgments for parenting mistakes
articles.summary: Working mothers who pursue career success are harshly judged for their parenting mistakes, while high-achieving fathers face no such scrutiny. A new study reveals how workplace ambition triggers moral condemnation that forces women to self-regulate.

articles.title: Learning a new skill triggers both temporary cell swelling and lasting structural growth in the human brain
articles.summary: When you learn a new skill, your brain undergoes physical changes. A new study using advanced MRI technology reveals that mastering a task triggers two distinct, unexpected cellular reactions that reshape our understanding of human neuroplasticity.

articles.title: APOE2 may protect the brain from Alzheimer’s and aging
articles.summary: The longevity-linked APOE2 gene appears to protect brain cells by reducing DNA damage and helping neurons recover from stress. The finding could open a new path toward treatments that mimic APOE2’s defenses in people at higher genetic risk for Alzheimer’s.

articles.title: New study links digital “brain rot” to a cascading sequence of psychological burdens
articles.summary: The passive consumption of endless short-form videos creates cognitive fatigue popularly known as brain rot. A new study reveals how this digital exhaustion initiates a psychological cascade of burnout, stress, and anxiety that ultimately precipitates depression.
